question: A tenant pays $900/month rent and gives a $950 security deposit. The tenant occupies the unit for 9 months before moving out. Does this deposit qualify for the interest requirement of ORC 5321.16?
choice_a: Yes -- the $950 deposit exceeds the greater of $50 or one month's rent ($900), and the tenancy ran at least six months
choice_b: No -- the deposit must exceed two months' rent to qualify, regardless of tenancy length
choice_c: No -- ORC 5321.16 only applies to deposits on commercial leases
choice_d: Yes, but only because the tenant paid rent on time every month
explanation: ORC 5321.16 requires interest once a deposit exceeds the greater of $50 or one month's periodic rent AND the tenancy has run at least six months; here the $950 deposit exceeds the $900 monthly-rent threshold and the tenant stayed nine months, so both prongs are satisfied.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A tenant pays $1,200 as a security deposit on a $1,000/month unit, but moves out after only 4 months. Under ORC 5321.16, is the landlord obligated to pay interest on that deposit?
choice_a: No -- even though the deposit exceeds one month's rent, the tenancy did not reach the required six-month minimum
choice_b: Yes -- any deposit over $1,000 accrues interest regardless of how long the tenant stays
choice_c: Yes -- interest accrues the moment the lease is signed
choice_d: No -- deposits under $2,000 never accrue interest in Ohio
explanation: ORC 5321.16's interest obligation requires both conditions to be met: the deposit must exceed the greater of $50 or one month's rent, and the tenancy must run at least six months. A four-month tenancy fails the durational prong even though the dollar threshold is exceeded, so no interest accrues.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A tenant on a 12-month lease pays $700/month rent and puts down a $700 security deposit -- exactly equal to one month's rent, not more. Under ORC 5321.16, must the landlord pay interest on this deposit even though the tenancy exceeds six months?
choice_a: No -- the statute requires the deposit to exceed the greater of $50 or one month's rent, and a deposit merely equal to one month's rent does not exceed that threshold
choice_b: Yes -- once the tenancy passes six months, interest applies regardless of the deposit's relationship to monthly rent
choice_c: Yes -- any deposit on a 12-month lease automatically qualifies
choice_d: No -- fixed-term leases of any deposit amount are exempt from ORC 5321.16 entirely
explanation: ORC 5321.16 requires the deposit to EXCEED the greater of $50 or one month's periodic rent. A deposit exactly equal to one month's rent does not exceed that figure, so the interest obligation is not triggered even though the six-month durational threshold would otherwise be satisfied.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A tenant's security deposit qualifies for interest under ORC 5321.16 at a principal amount of $1,000, and the tenant remains in the unit for exactly two full years. Applying the statutory 5% per annum simple-interest rate, how much interest has accrued by the end of the second year?
choice_a: $100 (5% of $1,000 for each of the two years, added together)
choice_b: $102.50 (5% compounded annually over two years)
choice_c: $50 total for the entire two-year period
choice_d: $200, because the rate doubles after the first year
explanation: ORC 5321.16 sets a flat 5% per annum SIMPLE interest rate, not compound interest. On a $1,000 qualifying deposit, that is $50 per year; over two years, simple interest totals $100 ($50 + $50), not a compounded amount.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A landlord calculates interest owed on a qualifying $2,000 security deposit by compounding the 5% rate monthly rather than applying it as simple annual interest. Is this calculation method consistent with ORC 5321.16?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.16 specifies simple interest at 5% per annum, not a compounded rate, so compounding overstates or understates what is actually owed
choice_b: Yes -- compounding is required whenever the deposit exceeds $1,000
choice_c: Yes -- landlords may choose either simple or compound interest at their discretion
choice_d: No -- ORC 5321.16 requires compounding daily, not monthly
explanation: ORC 5321.16 fixes the rate as 5% per annum on a SIMPLE-interest basis. A landlord who compounds the rate is not applying the statutory formula correctly, regardless of whether compounding happens to produce a higher or lower figure than the statute intends.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A landlord holds a qualifying interest-bearing security deposit throughout a tenant's three-year tenancy but never pays or credits any interest to the tenant during that entire period. Has the landlord complied with ORC 5321.16?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.16 requires the accrued interest to be paid or credited to the tenant annually, not deferred until the tenancy ends
choice_b: Yes -- the statute only requires interest to be paid once, at the very end of the tenancy
choice_c: Yes -- interest need only be paid if the tenant specifically requests it in writing
choice_d: No -- interest must be paid quarterly, not annually
explanation: ORC 5321.16 requires interest on a qualifying deposit to be paid or credited to the tenant on an ANNUAL basis, not held and paid only once at lease-end; a landlord who never pays or credits interest during three full years of an ongoing tenancy has not complied.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A tenant vacates and the landlord mails the deposit balance along with a written itemized list of deductions on day 45 after the rental agreement terminated. Has the landlord met the ORC 5321.16 deadline?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.16 requires the balance and itemized deductions to be returned within 30 days of termination and delivery of possession, and day 45 is outside that window
choice_b: Yes -- as long as the landlord mails it within 60 days, the deadline is satisfied
choice_c: Yes -- there is no fixed deadline as long as the landlord acts in good faith
choice_d: No -- the deadline is 10 days, so 45 days is a minor overage, not a violation
explanation: ORC 5321.16 sets a firm 30-day deadline, running from termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession, for the landlord to return the balance of the deposit together with a written itemization of any deductions. Returning it on day 45 falls outside that statutory window.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: When a landlord deducts $200 from a tenant's security deposit for cleaning costs, what must the landlord provide the tenant along with the remaining deposit balance under ORC 5321.16?
choice_a: A written, itemized list identifying the specific deductions made and the amounts, such as the $200 cleaning charge
choice_b: Nothing further -- the landlord need only return whatever balance remains, with no explanation required
choice_c: A notarized affidavit signed by a third-party inspector
choice_d: Photographic evidence filed with the county recorder's office
explanation: ORC 5321.16 requires the landlord to accompany any returned deposit balance with a written itemization identifying the specific deductions -- such as a $200 cleaning charge -- and their amounts, not merely to hand back whatever is left over unexplained.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A tenant properly gives the landlord a written forwarding address at move-out. The landlord nonetheless wrongfully withholds part of the deposit beyond the 30-day deadline. Under ORC 5321.16, is the tenant entitled to pursue damages and attorney fees?
choice_a: Yes -- because the tenant supplied the required written forwarding address, the tenant may pursue the full wrongful-withholding remedy of damages and attorney fees
choice_b: No -- providing a forwarding address only entitles the tenant to a refund of the deposit itself, never to damages or fees
choice_c: No -- the forwarding address requirement bars all remedies unless the tenant also files within 10 days
choice_d: Yes, but only if the withheld amount exceeds $1,000
explanation: ORC 5321.16 conditions the tenant's right to pursue damages and attorney fees for wrongful withholding on the tenant having supplied a written forwarding address. Having satisfied that condition, this tenant may pursue the full remedy against a landlord who wrongfully withholds the deposit.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: Does the landlord's basic 30-day obligation to return a tenant's security deposit balance under ORC 5321.16 depend on the tenant having first supplied a written forwarding address?
choice_a: No -- the 30-day return obligation itself is not conditioned on a forwarding address; only the tenant's ability to recover the added damages-plus-attorney-fees remedy for wrongful withholding depends on providing one
choice_b: Yes -- the landlord has no duty whatsoever to return any deposit until a forwarding address is received, no matter how much time passes
choice_c: Yes -- without a forwarding address, the landlord may keep the deposit permanently
choice_d: No -- forwarding addresses are irrelevant to any provision of ORC 5321.16
explanation: ORC 5321.16's underlying duty to return the deposit balance within 30 days applies regardless of a forwarding address. It is specifically the tenant's right to pursue the enhanced damages-plus-attorney-fees remedy for wrongful withholding that is conditioned on the tenant having given the landlord a written forwarding address.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A landlord wrongfully withholds $300 of a tenant's security deposit in violation of ORC 5321.16, and the tenant incurs $250 in reasonable attorney fees pursuing the claim. What is the landlord's total statutory exposure?
choice_a: $300 (the wrongfully withheld amount) + $300 (an equal amount as damages) + $250 (attorney fees) = $850
choice_b: Only the original $300 wrongfully withheld, with no additional damages or fees
choice_c: $900 (triple the withheld amount), with attorney fees waived
choice_d: $300 flat, plus a separate $50 statutory penalty regardless of attorney fees
explanation: ORC 5321.16 allows recovery of the amount wrongfully withheld plus an equal amount as damages, plus reasonable attorney fees. On these facts that is $300 + $300 + $250 = $850 total exposure for the landlord.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A landlord wrongfully withholds $750 of a tenant's deposit. Before any attorney fees are added, what dollar amount is the tenant entitled to recover under ORC 5321.16's wrongful-withholding remedy?
choice_a: $1,500 (the $750 wrongfully withheld plus an equal $750 in damages)
choice_b: $750 only, with damages capped at the original amount
choice_c: $2,250 (triple damages)
choice_d: $375 (half the withheld amount, as a penalty discount)
explanation: ORC 5321.16 doubles the wrongfully withheld amount as the baseline remedy -- the withheld sum plus an equal amount in damages -- before any attorney fees are even added, so $750 wrongfully withheld yields $1,500 in recoverable damages alone.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A landlord deducts $400 from a deposit for documented damage beyond normal move-out condition and properly itemizes it within 30 days. Does ORC 5321.16's wrongful-withholding remedy (withheld amount + equal damages + attorney fees) apply to this $400 deduction?
choice_a: No -- the wrongful-withholding remedy applies only to amounts withheld in violation of the statute; a properly itemized, timely, substantiated deduction is not 'wrongfully withheld'
choice_b: Yes -- any deduction from a deposit automatically triggers the doubling remedy
choice_c: Yes -- the remedy applies to the full original deposit amount, not just the disputed portion
choice_d: No -- ORC 5321.16's remedy never applies to any withheld amount under $500
explanation: ORC 5321.16's enhanced remedy targets deposit amounts wrongfully withheld -- meaning withheld in violation of the statute's procedural or substantive requirements. A properly itemized, timely deduction supported by actual damage is a legitimate deduction, not a wrongful withholding, so the doubling-plus-fees remedy is not implicated.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A landlord both misses the 30-day return deadline AND fails to provide any itemized list of deductions when eventually returning $600 of a tenant's deposit late. If the entire $600 is found to be wrongfully withheld, and the tenant supplied a forwarding address, what can the tenant recover under ORC 5321.16?
choice_a: $1,200 (the $600 wrongfully withheld plus an equal $600 in damages), plus reasonable attorney fees
choice_b: Only the original $600, with no additional remedy because the landlord eventually paid
choice_c: $600 plus a flat $100 late fee, with no attorney fees available
choice_d: Nothing -- late payment of a deposit balance is not independently actionable
explanation: Where the withheld deposit amount is wrongfully withheld -- here, through both a missed deadline and a missing itemization -- and the tenant has supplied a forwarding address, ORC 5321.16 entitles the tenant to the withheld amount plus an equal amount in damages plus reasonable attorney fees: $600 + $600 + fees.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: A tenant pays $1,000/month rent and a $1,100 security deposit -- exceeding the one-month-rent threshold -- and occupies the unit for exactly one qualifying year, with the deposit accruing the statutory 5% simple annual rate. How much interest must the landlord pay or credit for that year?
choice_a: $55 (5% of the $1,100 deposit)
choice_b: $110 (10% of the deposit)
choice_c: $11 (0.5% of the deposit, treating 5% as a decimal error)
choice_d: $0, because the deposit merely equals the threshold rather than exceeding it
explanation: Because the $1,100 deposit exceeds the $1,000 monthly-rent threshold and the tenancy qualifies at six-plus months (here a full year), ORC 5321.16's 5% per annum simple interest applies to the deposit principal: 5% of $1,100 is $55 for that year.
source_note: ORC 5321.16 (confirmed via memo research pass against codes.ohio.gov)

question: Under ORC 5321.04, if a tenant's lease purports to waive the landlord's duty to keep the premises in compliance with health and safety codes, is that lease provision enforceable?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.04 establishes an independent statutory floor for landlord duties that a private lease cannot waive below
choice_b: Yes -- landlords and tenants are always free to contract around any statutory landlord duty
choice_c: Yes, but only if the tenant is a commercial rather than residential tenant
choice_d: No -- but only because the lease was not notarized
explanation: ORC 5321.04 imposes a mandatory statutory floor of landlord obligations -- including code compliance and habitability repairs -- that exists independent of what the lease says; a lease clause purporting to waive these below the statutory minimum is not given effect.

question: A tenant reports a broken furnace to the landlord in January. Under ORC 5321.04, what is the landlord's basic obligation once notified of a defect materially affecting health and safety?
choice_a: To make repairs and do whatever is reasonably necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition
choice_b: Nothing -- heating repairs are always the tenant's sole responsibility
choice_c: To immediately terminate the tenant's lease rather than repair the furnace
choice_d: To reduce rent permanently in lieu of ever making the repair
explanation: ORC 5321.04 requires the landlord to make repairs and take reasonably necessary action to keep the premises fit and habitable, including addressing a broken furnace -- a defect materially affecting health and safety, particularly during winter months.

question: In late December, a landlord shuts off the furnace to a tenant's unit to save on utility costs, leaving the unit without heat for over a week. Does this violate the landlord's obligations under ORC 5321.04?
choice_a: Yes -- ORC 5321.04 requires the landlord to supply reasonable heat, and deliberately cutting it off during winter breaches that duty
choice_b: No -- heat is only required to be supplied between June and September
choice_c: No -- ORC 5321.04 makes heat entirely optional at the landlord's discretion
choice_d: Yes, but only if the lease specifically mentions heat
explanation: ORC 5321.04 requires a landlord to supply reasonable heat as one of the essential services owed to a tenant (subject to narrow exceptions such as tenant-controlled utility accounts). Deliberately cutting off heat during winter is a direct breach of that statutory duty.

question: Which of the following is explicitly NOT among the essential services ORC 5321.04 obligates a residential landlord to supply?
choice_a: Cable television service
choice_b: Reasonable heat
choice_c: Running water
choice_d: Reasonable amounts of hot water
explanation: ORC 5321.04 lists running water, reasonable hot water, and reasonable heat as essential services a landlord must supply (subject to certain exceptions). Cable television is not among the statute's enumerated essential services.

question: A landlord wants to inspect a tenant's unit for a routine, non-emergency maintenance check. The landlord gives the tenant 24 hours' notice and plans to enter at a reasonable hour. Is this consistent with ORC 5321.04?
choice_a: Yes -- 24 hours' notice is presumed reasonable for a non-emergency entry, and entering at a reasonable hour avoids abusing the right of access
choice_b: No -- any entry by the landlord requires the tenant's written consent obtained at least 7 days in advance
choice_c: No -- ORC 5321.04 bars landlord entry for any purpose other than eviction
choice_d: Yes, but only if the tenant is present and personally lets the landlord in
explanation: ORC 5321.04 presumes 24 hours' advance notice reasonable for landlord entry for a non-emergency purpose, and requires that entry not abuse the tenant's right of access -- meaning it should occur at a reasonable time. This scenario meets both conditions.

question: A pipe bursts in a tenant's unit at 2 a.m., flooding the apartment below. May the landlord enter the tenant's unit immediately, without providing the 24-hour notice ORC 5321.04 otherwise presumes reasonable?
choice_a: Yes -- ORC 5321.04's notice presumption applies to non-emergency entries; a genuine emergency such as an active flood justifies immediate entry without advance notice
choice_b: No -- the landlord must always wait the full 24 hours regardless of the circumstances
choice_c: No -- emergency entry is never permitted under Ohio law without a court order
choice_d: Yes, but only between the hours of 9 a.m. and 5 p.m.
explanation: ORC 5321.04's 24-hour notice presumption governs non-emergency entries. A genuine emergency -- such as an active burst pipe threatening property damage -- falls outside that presumption and permits the landlord to enter without advance notice.

question: A city housing inspector cites a rental unit for a code violation that is purely cosmetic (chipped paint on a fence, not affecting health or safety) and unrelated to habitability. Does ORC 5321.04 obligate the landlord to remedy this specific violation as a habitability duty?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.04's mandatory duty targets code violations that materially affect health and safety, not every conceivable code citation regardless of severity
choice_b: Yes -- ORC 5321.04 requires the landlord to cure every code citation of any kind, no matter how minor
choice_c: No -- ORC 5321.04 imposes no code-compliance duty on landlords whatsoever
choice_d: Yes, but only for violations cited by the state fire marshal specifically
explanation: ORC 5321.04's statutory duty is tied to codes materially affecting health and safety -- the habitability floor -- rather than to every possible code citation regardless of its connection to health or safety.

question: A tenant has arranged for the electric utility to bill the tenant directly, with the tenant's own account. Under ORC 5321.04, is the landlord still obligated to personally supply electricity as an essential service in this situation?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.04's essential-services duty has an exception where the tenant controls that utility directly with the utility provider
choice_b: Yes -- the landlord must supply and pay for all utilities regardless of who holds the account
choice_c: No -- ORC 5321.04 never requires landlords to supply electricity under any circumstance
choice_d: Yes, but only if the tenant requests it in writing
explanation: ORC 5321.04's essential-services obligation carves out situations where the tenant directly controls a utility with the utility provider (or where the building is not required by law to be equipped for that service), relieving the landlord of the duty to personally supply that service in those circumstances.

question: Which obligation below belongs to the LANDLORD under ORC 5321.04, rather than to the tenant under ORC 5321.05?
choice_a: Complying with codes materially affecting health and safety and keeping the premises fit and habitable
choice_b: Keeping the portion of the premises the tenant occupies safe and sanitary
choice_c: Disposing of the tenant's own rubbish and garbage in a clean, safe manner
choice_d: Using the tenant's own plumbing and electrical fixtures properly
explanation: ORC 5321.04 places the code-compliance and habitability-repair duty on the landlord, while ORC 5321.05 places reciprocal duties -- keeping the occupied space safe and sanitary, proper rubbish disposal, and proper fixture use -- on the tenant.

question: Under ORC 5321.05, besides keeping their portion of the premises safe and sanitary, what other obligation does the statute place on a tenant regarding fixtures within the unit?
choice_a: Using and operating all plumbing and electrical fixtures properly
choice_b: Personally replacing any fixture that becomes outdated, regardless of who caused the wear
choice_c: Insuring all fixtures against damage at the tenant's own expense
choice_d: Upgrading fixtures to current code standards before move-out
explanation: ORC 5321.05 requires a tenant to use and operate plumbing and electrical fixtures properly, in addition to keeping the occupied space safe and sanitary and disposing of rubbish and garbage appropriately.

question: Under ORC 5321.05, is a residential tenant obligated to comply with the housing, health, and safety codes that apply to the tenant's own conduct within the unit?
choice_a: Yes -- ORC 5321.05 imposes a tenant duty to comply with applicable housing, health, and safety code requirements, mirroring the landlord's own code-compliance duty
choice_b: No -- code compliance is exclusively the landlord's responsibility under all circumstances
choice_c: No -- tenants have no statutory duties whatsoever under ORC Chapter 5321
choice_d: Yes, but only for tenants in buildings with five or more units
explanation: ORC 5321.05 imposes reciprocal duties on tenants, including compliance with applicable housing, health, and safety code requirements as they pertain to the tenant's own use of the premises -- complementing, not replacing, the landlord's own code-compliance duty under ORC 5321.04.

question: A tenant repeatedly leaves garbage bags piled in a shared hallway rather than disposing of them properly, leading to a pest infestation. Whose statutory duty under ORC 5321.05 has most directly been breached?
choice_a: The tenant's -- ORC 5321.05 requires disposing of rubbish and garbage in a clean, safe manner
choice_b: The landlord's -- rubbish disposal is exclusively a landlord duty under ORC 5321.04
choice_c: Neither party has any duty regarding rubbish under Ohio law
choice_d: The tenant's, but only if the lease specifically addresses garbage disposal
explanation: ORC 5321.05 places the duty to dispose of rubbish and garbage in a clean and safe manner on the tenant. Improperly leaving garbage that causes a pest problem is a direct breach of that specific statutory tenant obligation.

question: A rental agreement clause states the tenant is personally responsible for repairing any structural defect discovered in the dwelling, at the tenant's own expense. Is this consistent with the tenant duties actually described in ORC 5321.05?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.05's tenant duties are limited to matters like keeping the occupied space safe and sanitary, proper rubbish disposal, and proper fixture use -- not structural repairs, which fall under the landlord's ORC 5321.04 habitability duty
choice_b: Yes -- ORC 5321.05 explicitly makes tenants responsible for all structural repairs
choice_c: Yes -- any lease clause automatically overrides the statutory duties in ORC 5321.05
choice_d: No -- ORC 5321.05 imposes no duties on tenants at all
explanation: ORC 5321.05's tenant duties are narrower than structural repair obligations -- they cover matters like sanitary upkeep of the occupied space, rubbish disposal, and proper fixture use. Structural repairs remain within the landlord's habitability duty under ORC 5321.04, which a lease clause cannot simply reassign to the tenant.

question: A landlord owns a duplex, occupies one of the two units personally, and has given the tenant proper statutory disclosure of that fact. Under ORC 5321.07, how does this affect the tenant's ability to invoke the section's rent-escrow and repair remedies?
choice_a: ORC 5321.07 exempts landlords of owner-occupied properties with three units or fewer -- with proper disclosure -- from the section's remedy scheme
choice_b: It has no effect; ORC 5321.07 applies identically to every residential landlord regardless of occupancy or unit count
choice_c: It doubles the cure period the tenant must allow before pursuing remedies
choice_d: It bars the tenant from ever contacting a housing code inspector
explanation: ORC 5321.07 exempts landlords of small, owner-occupied properties of three units or fewer -- where the landlord has given the tenant proper disclosure -- from the rent-escrow and repair-order remedy scheme the section otherwise makes available to tenants.

question: A tenant lives in a dormitory-style student housing arrangement covered by an ORC 5321.07 exemption for certain student housing. What is the practical effect of that exemption?
choice_a: The tenant cannot invoke ORC 5321.07's specific rent-escrow-and-repair-order remedy scheme against that landlord
choice_b: The tenant automatically loses all rights under every section of ORC Chapter 5321
choice_c: The landlord is exempted from ORC 5321.04's basic habitability duties as well
choice_d: The exemption only applies during summer break
explanation: ORC 5321.07 carves out an exemption for certain student housing landlords from that section's specific remedy scheme (rent escrow, court-ordered repairs, or termination), though this is a narrower exemption from ORC 5321.07 itself, not a blanket exemption from the landlord's other statutory duties.

question: A tenant stops paying rent entirely after noticing a leaking roof, without ever sending the landlord written notice of the problem. May this tenant invoke ORC 5321.07's remedies against the landlord?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.07 conditions a tenant's remedies on first giving the landlord written notice of the specific noncompliance and allowing a reasonable cure period
choice_b: Yes -- a tenant may always withhold rent immediately upon discovering any defect, with no notice required
choice_c: Yes -- because the roof leak is severe, the notice requirement is automatically waived
choice_d: No -- ORC 5321.07 never allows a tenant to withhold rent under any circumstances
explanation: ORC 5321.07 requires the tenant to first give the landlord written notice specifying the noncompliance and to allow a reasonable time (or 30 days, whichever is sooner) to cure it, before exercising further remedies. A tenant who withholds rent without ever giving that notice has not satisfied the statutory prerequisite.

question: A tenant gives the landlord written notice of a broken water heater. The landlord repairs it within two weeks, well inside the statutory cure period. May the tenant still pursue ORC 5321.07's rent-escrow or termination remedies over that same issue?
choice_a: No -- once the landlord cures the noncompliance within the reasonable time (or 30-day) period, the tenant's basis for invoking the further ORC 5321.07 remedies over that issue is resolved
choice_b: Yes -- the tenant may still terminate the lease even after a timely repair, with no further justification needed
choice_c: Yes -- the cure period is irrelevant once a tenant has sent any written notice
choice_d: No -- but only because two weeks happens to be an unusually fast repair
explanation: ORC 5321.07's remedy scheme is triggered by the landlord's failure to cure noncompliance within a reasonable time or 30 days, whichever is sooner. Where the landlord in fact cures within that window, the statutory basis for the tenant to pursue rent escrow, a repair order, or termination over that specific issue no longer applies.

question: A tenant is two months behind on rent when a plumbing problem arises. Under ORC 5321.07, can this tenant invoke the section's rent-escrow or repair-order remedies while delinquent on rent?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.07's remedies are available only to a tenant who is current on rent
choice_b: Yes -- rent status is irrelevant to eligibility for ORC 5321.07 remedies
choice_c: Yes, as long as the tenant pays the back rent within 90 days after invoking the remedy
choice_d: No -- but only because the arrears exceed one month's rent specifically
explanation: ORC 5321.07's rent-escrow and related remedies are limited to a tenant who is current on rent (a 'rent-current tenant'); a tenant behind on rent is not eligible to invoke this particular remedy scheme over an unrelated maintenance issue.

question: A tenant falls behind on rent by several months due to a job loss and never catches up. Even if the landlord is separately violating ORC 5321.04 by failing to make necessary repairs, can this tenant still invoke ORC 5321.07's court deposit-and-repair-order remedy?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.07's specific remedy scheme requires the tenant to be current on rent, so a tenant with unpaid back rent cannot invoke this particular avenue regardless of the landlord's own noncompliance
choice_b: Yes -- landlord noncompliance always excuses a tenant's own rent-current requirement
choice_c: Yes -- ORC 5321.07 has no rent-current requirement at all
choice_d: No -- but only if the arrears exceed $5,000
explanation: ORC 5321.07's rent-escrow and repair-order remedy is expressly limited to a rent-current tenant. A tenant who has fallen behind on rent -- even where the landlord is separately noncompliant -- cannot invoke this specific statutory remedy while in arrears.

question: A tenant falls three months behind on rent. Rather than filing an eviction action, the landlord personally shuts off the water to the unit to pressure the tenant to leave. Is this consistent with ORC 5321.15?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.15 bans self-help eviction measures such as utility shutoffs regardless of how far behind on rent the tenant is; the landlord must use the formal eviction process
choice_b: Yes -- once a tenant is more than two months behind, self-help measures become lawful
choice_c: Yes -- utility shutoffs are permitted as long as the landlord gives 24 hours' notice first
choice_d: No -- but only because water, specifically, is exempt from the self-help ban while other utilities are not
explanation: ORC 5321.15 prohibits self-help measures such as utility shutoffs to regain possession, no matter how delinquent the tenant is on rent; a landlord must instead pursue the formal court eviction process under Chapters 1923, 5303, and 5321.

question: While a tenant is away for a weekend trip, the landlord changes the locks and moves the tenant's belongings into storage without a court order. Under ORC 5321.15, what is the tenant's civil remedy against the landlord for this conduct?
choice_a: The tenant may recover actual damages caused by the unlawful self-help eviction, plus reasonable attorney fees
choice_b: The tenant has no civil remedy because the landlord did not physically harm the tenant
choice_c: The tenant's only remedy is to file a police report; no civil action is available
choice_d: The tenant may only recover the cost of a locksmith to change the locks back
explanation: ORC 5321.15 makes a landlord who engages in self-help eviction -- such as changing locks or removing belongings without going through the court process -- civilly liable for the tenant's actual damages plus reasonable attorney fees.

question: Under ORC 5321.15, the formal procedures a landlord must use to lawfully regain possession of residential premises are found across which group of Ohio Revised Code chapters?
choice_a: Chapters 1923, 5303, and 5321
choice_b: Chapters 4735 and 4112 only
choice_c: Chapter 5302 exclusively
choice_d: Chapter 323 (real property taxation) exclusively
explanation: ORC 5321.15 prohibits regaining possession outside the formal eviction procedures established across ORC Chapters 1923 (forcible entry and detainer), 5303 (actions concerning real property), and 5321 (Landlord-Tenant Act) itself.

question: A signed lease includes a clause stating the landlord 'may re-enter and retake possession by any means necessary, including changing locks, without resort to court process.' Under ORC 5321.15, is this clause enforceable to authorize self-help eviction?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.15's self-help eviction ban applies regardless of any lease clause purporting to authorize it
choice_b: Yes -- parties are free to contract around the self-help eviction ban if both sign the lease voluntarily
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial tenancies, not residential ones
choice_d: No -- but only because the clause fails to mention locks specifically
explanation: ORC 5321.15's prohibition on self-help eviction is not waivable by lease language; a clause purporting to authorize the landlord to bypass the formal court eviction process is unenforceable, and a landlord who acts on it remains civilly liable.

question: A landlord wants to end a month-to-month tenancy without alleging any breach by the tenant. Under ORC 5321.17, how must the required 30 days' notice be timed?
choice_a: It must be given at least 30 days prior to the periodic rental date on which the tenancy would otherwise renew
choice_b: It must be given exactly 30 calendar days before the landlord personally decides to end the tenancy, regardless of the rental date
choice_c: It may be given at any time, as long as the tenant vacates within 30 days of receiving it
choice_d: It must be given 30 days after the tenant's most recent rent payment
explanation: ORC 5321.17 requires that notice to terminate or not renew a month-to-month tenancy be given at least 30 days prior to the periodic rental date -- the date on which the periodic term would otherwise renew -- not simply 30 days before an arbitrary decision date.

question: A landlord seeks to terminate a tenancy because the tenant has materially breached the rental agreement, rather than simply ending a periodic tenancy without cause. Do ORC 5321.17's 7-day/30-day notice tiers apply to this breach-based termination?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.17's notice-period requirements govern terminations of periodic tenancies made WITHOUT cause; they do not apply where termination is instead based on a breach of the rental agreement or of a statutory duty
choice_b: Yes -- every termination in Ohio, breach-based or not, must follow the exact 7-day or 30-day notice tiers
choice_c: No -- breach-based terminations require no notice of any kind, ever
choice_d: Yes, but only if the breach involves nonpayment of rent specifically
explanation: ORC 5321.17's 7-day (week-to-week) and 30-day (month-to-month) notice tiers apply to terminations of a periodic tenancy without cause. Where termination instead rests on a breach of the rental agreement or of a statutory duty, this particular notice-period requirement does not govern.

question: A tenant on a week-to-week tenancy decides to move out and wants to give proper notice to the landlord. Under ORC 5321.17, how much advance notice must this TENANT give?
choice_a: At least 7 days prior to the termination date -- the same notice period applies whether the landlord or the tenant is the one ending a week-to-week tenancy
choice_b: At least 30 days, because tenant-initiated terminations always require longer notice than landlord-initiated ones
choice_c: No notice is required from a tenant, only from a landlord
choice_d: At least 24 hours, matching the entry-notice standard under ORC 5321.04
explanation: ORC 5321.17 sets a reciprocal 7-day notice period for terminating or not renewing a week-to-week tenancy, applicable to either the landlord or the tenant -- a tenant ending a week-to-week tenancy owes the same 7 days' notice a landlord would owe.

question: How does the 3-or-more-days' notice required under ORC 1923.04 before filing an eviction lawsuit differ in purpose from the 7-day/30-day notice tiers under ORC 5321.17?
choice_a: ORC 1923.04's notice is the prerequisite before actually filing an eviction action in court, while ORC 5321.17's notice governs ending a periodic tenancy without cause (before any eviction filing is even at issue)
choice_b: They are the same requirement described twice, with no functional difference
choice_c: ORC 5321.17 only applies to commercial leases, while ORC 1923.04 only applies to residential leases
choice_d: ORC 1923.04's notice applies only to landlords, while ORC 5321.17's notice applies only to tenants
explanation: ORC 1923.04's three-or-more-days' notice is the precondition a landlord must satisfy before filing a forcible entry and detainer (eviction) action in court. ORC 5321.17's 7-day/30-day tiers instead govern how a periodic tenancy is terminated or not renewed without cause, a distinct step that may precede resorting to the eviction process at all.

question: A landlord sends a month-to-month tenant a notice ending the tenancy, but the notice is delivered only 15 days before the next periodic rental date and alleges no breach by the tenant. Does this notice satisfy ORC 5321.17?
choice_a: No -- ORC 5321.17 requires at least 30 days' notice prior to the periodic rental date to end a month-to-month tenancy without cause, and 15 days falls short
choice_b: Yes -- any advance notice at all is sufficient as long as it is given in writing
choice_c: Yes -- 15 days is sufficient because it exceeds the 7-day minimum for week-to-week tenancies
choice_d: No -- but only because the notice was not notarized
explanation: ORC 5321.17 requires at least 30 days' notice, given prior to the periodic rental date, to terminate or decline to renew a month-to-month tenancy without cause. A notice giving only 15 days' advance warning does not meet that statutory minimum.
